findings.body:
The change replaces the parameterized query (placeholder `?` with `params: vec![name]`) with `format!` that interpolates `name` directly into the SQL text inside single quotes, and sets `params` to `Vec::new()`. A `name` containing `'` changes the SQL structure, and nothing escapes or binds it.

Trigger: find_user is called with a name containing a single quote or other SQL syntax, for example O'Brien or ' OR '1'='1.

Impact: Any caller passing untrusted input to find_user gets SQL injection: attackers can read other rows or other tables, or alter the statement. Names with quotes also produce malformed SQL errors for ordinary users.
findings.suggestion: Restore the placeholder form: text: "SELECT id FROM users WHERE name = ?".to_string(), params: vec![name.to_string()].
findings.title: User input interpolated into SQL, bypassing bound parameters

findings.body:
find_user now builds the SQL text with format!, inserting the raw `name` between single quotes (line 8) instead of keeping the `?` placeholder. The bound parameter list is now empty (line 9), so the name is never sent as a bound value. Any caller that executes `Query.text` as SQL gets the user input as part of the statement, and a quote in `name` ends the literal and changes the query.

Trigger: A caller passes a name containing a single quote or SQL syntax, for example `x' OR '1'='1`, and executes the returned Query.text.=

Impact: SQL injection for any caller of find_user that passes untrusted input and runs the returned query. An attacker could read or modify other rows or tables, or bypass the name filter.
findings.suggestion: Restore the parameterized form: text: "SELECT id FROM users WHERE name = ?".to_string(), params: vec![name.to_string()].
findings.title: find_user interpolates name into SQL text, enabling injection

risk_level.reason: The change replaces a parameterized SQL query with string interpolation of user input, introducing a SQL injection vulnerability in find_user.
